extracted_by: hand, T-0261 — the Chicago American read, June to August 1835
note: Volume I, Number 12, and the richest issue in the run for this project. Five lumber cargoes in six days name the rivers they came from; a land notice describes ground seven miles out as 'the oak woods … one third timbered, the balance prairie'; SARAH D. HOWE takes a room in Dr. Austin's house opposite Dr. Temple's — the run's only woman proprietor and its only doubly-anchored placement; the Reading Room's books are lodged somewhere while it waits for a building; and the Circuit Court's October term at Chicago is advertised with its clerk named.

claims.notes: THE ONLY WOMAN PROPRIETOR IN THE RUN, AND THE ONLY PLACEMENT WITH TWO ANCHORS. Sarah D. Howe takes a room in the house occupied by Dr. Austin — the botanic physician 1835-08-08 places ON LAKE STREET, NEAR THE POST OFFICE — and describes it as OPPOSITE Dr. Temple's. Three documented tenancies now triangulate on one spot: a doctor's house with a dressmaker's room in it, a second doctor's premises across the street, and the post office nearby. That is a piece of streetscape this project could actually build. THE STREET WORD IN HER OWN SENTENCE IS CUT ('taken a room a street'), so no street is recorded on the business; Lake Street comes from Austin's card and belongs there, not here. SHE IS ALSO HIRING: four or five young ladies wanted as apprentices, which documents a small workshop and not a one-woman room.

claims.notes: FIVE LUMBER CARGOES IN SIX DAYS, AND THEY NAME THEIR RIVERS. The Juliet from St. Joseph, the Bridget from KALAMAZOO, the Hiram from the CHIPPEWA and the Jesse Smith from the MENOMINEE — the Michigan and Wisconsin sawmill rivers, delivering into Chicago at roughly one cargo a day in the last week of August 1835. This project builds a town of sawn lumber and has reasoned about its supply from general history; here is the supply, named river by river and counted. Salt comes in from Oswego on Lake Ontario, merchandize from Buffalo, passengers from Green Bay, and a steamer from Buffalo via Green Bay. Two new hulls this week — the schooner Queen Charlotte and the steamboat Munroe. The arrival dates in this printing carry no month and are read as August from the issue's own date; that reading is bracketed throughout.

claims.notes: LAND COVER SEVEN MILES OUT OF CHICAGO, STATED AS A FRACTION: 160 acres 'in the oak woods, about 7 miles from Chicago — one third timbered, the balance [prairie]'. That is the single most useful sentence in the run for this project's timber and treeline work, which has had to argue the woodland/prairie boundary from maps and inference: here is a seller, with every reason to describe his own ground accurately, saying that a named distance out the oak woods are a THIRD timbered and the rest open. A second notice describes county land as 'about two-thirds timber land' near the contemplated Illinois and Michigan canal. WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED: neither parcel is placed by direction from town, and the word after 'the balance' is cut — 'prairie' is the supply the phrase demands and it is bracketed. The section number in the first is destroyed. Recorded as `street` rather than `building` because it describes ground, not structures.

business.name: A. Garrett, auctioneer
business.trade: auction of town lots and land

claims.notes: THE LAND BOOM WORKING THROUGH A CHICAGO AUCTION ROOM, and outward. A. Garrett — whose South Water Street store Montgomery took over in July and who signs from No. 1 Dearborn street on 1835-08-15 — is selling lots in a town of KANKAKEE that does not exist yet, fifty miles off at a river junction, AND advertising that his agent leaves next week for New York and the eastern states with fifteen or twenty plats to sell Chicago lots there. That is the machinery of the 1835 speculation described by one of its operators, and it is the context every land notice in this run sits in. Two auction rooms and two auctioneers are now documented on adjoining streets within six weeks.

claims.notes: THE READING ROOM STILL HAS NO ROOM, seven weeks after its directors met at the Tremont House to plan a building on the Public Square. Its books are 'for the present deposited at [?] House' — a hotel or private house whose name is cut — where members may see them. So the sequence this run documents is complete and negative: an association exists, it has books, it has directors and a secretary, and through the whole summer of 1835 it has nowhere of its own. Anything the reconstruction puts on the Public Square for a reading room at the scene date is wrong.

claims.notes: THE COURT SITS AT CHICAGO, and its calendar is published: the Cook County Circuit Court's next term opens on the first Monday of October 1835, with Richard J. Hamilton as clerk. This issue carries TWO divorce bills in chancery in identical form, both requiring absent defendants to appear. The parties' names are cut or garbled in both and NO private person is minted from them — naming someone as a divorce respondent on single-pass OCR of a damaged legal notice is the one place in this corpus where a wrong reading would do real harm to a real family's record. What is recorded is the institution: a county court sitting in this town on a stated date, and its clerk.

business.name: the Chicago American, newspaper and job printing office

claims.notes: THE AMERICAN'S OWN SHOP, ADVERTISING ITSELF — which is what the ticket asks for and the closest the run comes to an imprint that a locator can reach. Eleven weeks after its first issue the paper has just taken delivery of a large addition to its stock of printing materials and is selling job work: cards, deeds, bonds, mortgages and blanks, kept on hand and printed at short notice, with orders taken from the country. Read with 1835-06-08's editorial note that the paper could not publish earlier because its materials had only just arrived, this is a printing office equipping itself across the summer. The street on the business is Water Street, from Frederick Thomas's card of 1835-06-20 placing his store 'two doors from the American office' a little west of the bridge in Water street; the placement itself is left `none` because that address is somebody else's sentence, not the paper's.
